title: AI 陪伴游戏的留存机制拆解

Retention in an AI Companion Game Deconstructed — Deconstructor of Fun
0
Retention in an AI Companion Game Deconstructed
AI
Aug 24
Written By
Aylin Yazıcı
Written by
Harper Zhu
, co-founder and CPO of Kotoko AI, the studio behind Bside (iOS, Android, Steam). Before founding the studio, she spent seven years in game design at Tencent, FunPlus, Moonton, and Yahaha Studios. She also judges the DevGAMM Awards 2026.
AI companion apps are one of mobile's fastest-growing categories, and, by most operators' accounts, one of the hardest to retain. Cross-category mobile benchmarks sit at roughly
26% D1 and 11–13% D7
(Android at 11% to a 13% all-platform average, per
Adjust
). Most companion products are built conversation-first, and most struggle to hold those bars once launch spikes fade.
Bside
took the opposite bet, and it’s holding: ~60% D1 and ~25% D7
(internal data, mobile, July 2026; helped by strong growth in Japan). As a co-founder and CPO of
Kotoko AI
, the studio behind Bside, I stand behind these numbers
.
That's more than double the D1 benchmark and comfortably above the D7 bar. Bside launched on iOS and Android in March 2026; a Steam companion (October 2025) extends the same characters to the desktop, where they live on screen while you work. All data in this piece is mobile. Players build an original character from personality tags and a free-text description, then raise them. The game's job is to give them a life worth raising.
View fullsize
The loop is simple to describe. You create a character. You tend to them daily: dress them, gift them, check their feed. And you do things together: adventures, stories you write for them, vlogs they star in. Everything they do becomes a memory. The more they hold, the more there is to come back to.
Chat exists. The character remembers what you tell them. But conversation is deliberately not the front door. The retention pattern below points to that decision.
Nearly half of our players never open chat
In July, 41% of Bside's monthly active players never opened chat. Not once all month.
And in June, before Japan (our most chat-loving market) arrived, it was 49%..
View fullsize
Most of our users don’t use chat. Every path into chat is logged. This isn't a tracking gap.
For a product marketed and understood as an AI companion,
half the base ignoring the flagship category feature should be a scandal
. It stops being one if conversation was never the load-bearing wall. These players still engage with their character. They just spend that time doing things
with
them instead of talking
to
them.
The pattern sharpens when you cut daily activities by what you did that day:
View fullsize
Adventure days (including official content and player-made stories) beat chat days on 7-day return by 5.4 percentage points in all 24 of the daily cohorts old enough to have a full 7-day window.
One caveat: these are correlations instead of an experiment. Adventures are the deepest feature, so they select invested players. Dress-up is the broadest and most casual surface, so its number reads lower by composition. But the gap never flipped once. More importantly, it survived a market shift: after our Japan launch on July 17, adventure days kept beating chat days, and
the pattern held when we split players by market.
Whatever is driving it, it isn't one market's taste.
So what are the mechanics that make "raising" retain where "chatting" churns? Four things carry it.
Retention Mechanic #1: Authoring makes the character an asset
Every
Bside
player builds their character from scratch: a name, personality tags, and a free-text description.
There are no preset characters and no NPCs.
The tags aren’t cosmetic: they drive how the character behaves, what they post, and how they play through adventures.
View fullsize
This is the same investment psychology behind avatar editors and
Animal Crossing
villagers, pushed one level deeper: the player authors the
personality
, then watches them act.
The first session is the down payment that every later return protects.
A character you designed becomes a loss-aversion with a face.
Retention Mechanic #2: A life that runs while you're away
The character doesn’t freeze between sessions. They post about their day in a feed: small updates, moods, things they “did.” The posts pile up whether or not the player shows up.
Deconstructor of Fun covered this pattern in
the Finch widget deconstruction
: presence beats prompting. Finch’s estimated 54%/37% D1/D7 shows how far pet-raising mechanics can carry retention, even outside games.
Finch
applies this pattern to wellness; in the companion category, the effect can become the whole product. A pet that visibly lives while you’re at work creates a check-in impulse no push notification can fake.
Bside
’s feed is the same mechanic with authored personality on top. You’re checking what
your
character said.
Presence is also the cheapest AI surface we run
: a feed post costs a fraction of a conversation and stays visible all day.
Retention Mechanic #3: Stories give the relationship stakes — and players write them too
Adventures are branching story sessions where the character acts on the personality their player gave them.
Bside
’s appointment-and-payoff is layered like
Finch
’s adventuring cycle or a timer-gated chest. The difference is what the payoff is made of:
you find out who your character is under pressure.
This is where our stickiest players show up: on adventure days, nearly 30% are back seven days later.
View fullsize
And the stories run both directions. Adventures are authored by the game: we write the scenarios, the character acts, and the player chooses. In
Playground
, the player takes the pen: a visual-novel editor for staging scenes from their character’s life, from daily vignettes to full arcs.
Since the July launch, a striking share of player time has gone into it, especially in Japan. The design point is identical either way: stories give the character
consequence.
